body:
What is generative artificial intelligence?

Generative AI refers to AI systems that produce new content by learning patterns from existing data. Depending on the model, the output may be text, an image, audio, video or another form of content.

A traditional classification system may examine an image and predict whether it shows a cat or a dog. A generative system may instead create a new image of a cat from a written description. The first task selects a category; the second produces content.

Classification predicts which category an input belongs to. Generation produces new content. Both are AI tasks, but they are not the same task.

What is a large language model?

A large language model (LLM) is a machine-learning model trained on large amounts of language data to work with patterns in sequences of text. Many modern LLMs are built using deep-learning methods and can carry out several language tasks through instructions written in ordinary language.

Common tasks include answering questions, drafting passages, summarising information, translating language and rewriting sentences. The ability to perform these tasks does not mean the model independently verifies every factual statement.

Tokens and the generation of text

Language models process text using smaller units called tokens. A token may represent a complete word, part of a word or, in some systems, a character. A token is therefore not always equal to one word.

During text generation, a language model uses the prompt and available context to estimate suitable next tokens. It repeatedly selects tokens to build a response. The result can be grammatically fluent because the model has learned many relationships among language patterns.

Foundation models and pre-training

A foundation model is a broadly trained model that can support many tasks rather than being developed for only one narrow application. For example, a language foundation model may be used for summarisation, translation, drafting and question answering. A specialised system may adapt it for a particular purpose.

Pre-training is the broad initial training stage in which a model learns patterns from large amounts of data. Fine-tuning is additional training used to adapt an existing model to a more specific task or type of material.

Foundation models are not limited to text. Some are designed to work with more than one type of data, such as text and images. Such systems are described as multimodal.

Training, prompting and inference are different

When a user enters a prompt asking an LLM to summarise a paragraph, the model is generally performing inference. It uses its existing learned patterns to produce the summary.

The prompt provides instructions or context for the current interaction. Writing a better prompt can improve the usefulness of the response, but ordinary prompting does not by itself mean that the model's underlying parameters have been retrained.

By contrast, fine-tuning involves an additional training process that modifies the model. This distinction is important because a system may respond to new instructions without permanently learning them.

Capabilities and limitations

LLMs can help prepare drafts, explain familiar concepts, translate passages and organise information. However, they may misunderstand context, reproduce biases, provide outdated information or invent facts. Their fluent language is evidence of effective language generation, not proof that every statement is true.

Training and using large models can also require considerable computing power and electricity. A larger model is not automatically the most reliable or efficient choice for every task.

Prelims focus

  • Generative AI produces content such as text, images or audio.
  • LLM stands for large language model.
  • Tokens may be words, parts of words or characters.
  • A foundation model can support several tasks after broad training.
  • Pre-training and fine-tuning are training activities; ordinary prompt-based use is generally inference.
  • Trap: Giving an LLM a new prompt does not necessarily retrain the model or make its answer factually correct.

[Sources: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, 'Introduction to Large Language Models,' page summary and discussion of tokens and context (consulted 4 November 2026); 'LLMs: What's a Large Language Model?,' discussion of transformers and model limitations (consulted 4 November 2026); 'LLMs: Fine-tuning, Distillation, and Prompt Engineering,' discussion of foundation models, fine-tuning and prompting (consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: The prompt and paragraph become context; a model uses learned patterns to generate tokens repeatedly, forming a summary without searching for a prewritten answer.
pictures.caption: A language model generates text in tokens using its learned patterns and the supplied context.

title: Generative AI, Foundation Models and Large Language Models

body:
The meaning of hallucination in AI

An AI hallucination occurs when an AI system produces information that appears plausible but is false, unsupported or fabricated. The problem is especially noticeable in generative AI tools because they can present inaccurate information in clear, confident language.

For example, an LLM may invent the title of a government report, provide an incorrect date for a scheme or describe a research finding that the cited study does not contain. A fabricated source may look convincing even when it does not exist.

AI hallucination: An output that appears meaningful or credible but contains false, fabricated or unsupported information.

Why hallucinations occur

A language model learns patterns from training data and generates text that fits the prompt and its available context. It is not automatically connected to a verified, continuously updated record of every fact. Producing a likely sequence of words is different from demonstrating that a statement is true.

Hallucinations may become more likely when a question is ambiguous, relevant information is missing, the subject has changed since training or the model is asked to provide details that it cannot reliably establish.

The problem should not be confused with every ordinary software error. A system that fails to open a document or receives an incorrect measurement may have a different kind of failure. Hallucination specifically concerns the production of misleading, unsupported or fabricated content.

Why the risk matters

An invented date may cause a learner to remember an incorrect fact. A fabricated legal reference may mislead a reader about a rule. In healthcare, inaccurate information may be especially harmful if acted upon without professional checking.

The same principle applies to public administration: an automatically generated summary of a government circular should not replace examination of the actual circular when an official decision depends on its contents.

How to use generative AI more safely

Several practices can reduce the risk of accepting a hallucination:

  • Use reliable primary sources: Check dates, figures, legal provisions and programme details against original government documents or other authoritative records.
  • Check whether a cited source exists: A realistic-looking document title or reference is not proof that the document is genuine.
  • Check whether the source supports the claim: A real document may be quoted incorrectly or cited for something it does not establish.
  • Provide clear context: A precise question and relevant source material can reduce ambiguity.
  • Keep human review: Important conclusions should be checked by a suitably informed person before use.

Providing a model with relevant documents at the time of answering may improve factual grounding. However, the model can still misunderstand those documents or produce incorrect statements. No single prompting or verification technique guarantees the complete elimination of hallucinations.

Prelims focus

  • Hallucinations are plausible-looking but false, fabricated or unsupported AI outputs.
  • LLM text generation is not the same as verification against an authoritative source.
  • Fluent wording and confident presentation do not guarantee factual accuracy.
  • Supplying relevant source material can reduce risk but does not guarantee correctness.
  • Trap: An AI-generated citation should not be accepted merely because it contains a realistic title, date or document number.

[Sources: IBM, 'What Are AI Hallucinations?,' sections 'AI hallucinations, explained' and 'Why do AI hallucinations occur?,' updated 31 July 2026 (consulted 4 November 2026); Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, 'LLMs: What's a Large Language Model?,' discussion of model limitations (consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: In healthcare, AI-generated information requires verification before use.

pictures.alt: Check that the cited government document exists, then that it supports the exact launch date and claim; retain only the verified fact with its source.

title: AI Hallucinations: Why Fluent Answers May Be Incorrect

body:
What makes AI responsible?

Responsible AI means developing and using artificial intelligence in ways that protect people, reduce avoidable harm and ensure appropriate accountability. A useful AI system should not be judged only by how quickly it gives answers. Its reliability, fairness, privacy protections and effects on people also matter.

Responsible AI is especially important where a system may influence education, healthcare, employment or access to public services.

Bias and fairness

Bias in AI refers to systematic problems that can produce unfair or distorted results. Bias can arise from the data used for training, the way a problem is defined or the conditions in which a system is deployed. It does not always require deliberate discrimination by a developer.

Consider a speech-recognition tool trained mainly on recordings from one language variety. It may recognise some accents accurately but perform poorly for people speaking another accent or dialect. If the tool is used for a public service, the difference in accuracy could create unequal access.

Reducing harmful bias may involve collecting more representative data, evaluating performance across relevant groups, investigating errors and improving the system. High average accuracy is not enough if important groups experience substantially worse results.

Privacy and protection of personal information

AI systems may process names, photographs, voice recordings, examination records or other personal information. Some information, such as medical records, is especially sensitive.

Privacy protection includes limiting the collection and use of personal information to what is genuinely needed, obtaining appropriate permission or another lawful basis for processing, controlling access and protecting stored information. People should understand how their information will be used when it is collected.

For example, a teacher using a public AI chatbot to prepare practice questions generally does not need to upload a student's name, phone number and complete examination record. Removing unnecessary identifying details reduces exposure of personal information.

An AI tool may be useful without being suitable for confidential information. Users should not assume that information entered into every AI service remains private or is deleted immediately.

Transparency, explainability and accountability

Transparency means providing appropriate information about the use of AI, its purpose, relevant limitations and who is responsible for it. People affected by a decision should not be misled into believing that a machine-generated decision was independently examined by a person when it was not.

Explainability concerns the ability to provide understandable reasons or relevant information about how a system reached an output. Some complex models are more difficult to explain than simpler systems.

Accountability means that identifiable people or organisations remain responsible for developing, using and supervising the system. Responsibility does not disappear merely because software generated a recommendation.

Human oversight and meaningful review

Human oversight means that suitably responsible people can monitor AI use, examine important outputs, correct mistakes and intervene when necessary. In high-stakes situations, oversight should be meaningful rather than a formality.

For example, AI may help identify students who could benefit from extra academic support. A teacher should still consider the student's circumstances and check the evidence before deciding what assistance is appropriate. An AI prediction should not automatically become a final judgment about a student's ability.

Safety, resources and wider effects

Responsible AI also includes protecting systems against misuse, checking reliability under real operating conditions and considering wider effects. Training and operating large models can consume electricity and computing resources. AI may change the nature of work and create a need for new skills. These effects should be considered alongside possible benefits.

Recognised international guidance

UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence was adopted in November 2021. It emphasises human rights and human dignity, transparency, fairness, privacy and human oversight.

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published the AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 in 2023. It identifies characteristics of trustworthy AI, including validity and reliability, safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability, privacy enhancement and fairness with harmful bias managed.

These are guidance frameworks. Their existence does not mean that every AI system automatically satisfies the principles or that every recommendation is a directly enforceable law in India.

Prelims focus

  • Bias may result from unrepresentative training data or unsuitable system design.
  • Privacy protection includes limiting unnecessary collection and disclosure of personal information.
  • Transparency concerns openness about AI use and limitations; explainability concerns understanding an output.
  • Human oversight retains meaningful human review and intervention.
  • UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in November 2021.
  • NIST published AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 in 2023.
  • Trap: High overall accuracy does not automatically establish fairness for every group.

[Sources: NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023), section 3, 'AI Risks and Trustworthiness' (consulted 4 November 2026); UNESCO, 'Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence,' sections 'Core values' and 'Core principles' (consulted 4 November 2026); Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, 'Fairness: Identifying Bias' (consulted 4 November 2026).]
